TIME: 0.25 minutes

PURPOSE OF THIS LESSON
In Lesson 1, learners were introduced to the anchoring phenomenon — the healing cut — and began asking questions about why different cells look and behave differently. Lesson 2 establishes the conceptual foundation: every cell, no matter how specialised, is governed by the same cell theory. By building Version 1 of their cumulative cell model today, learners create a baseline they will revise in every subsequent lesson as they discover how structure drives function.

BEFORE CLASS
Prepare the class Driving Question Board, notebooks, coloured pencils, timer and paper slips. Provide 12 pre-cut feature cards per group of four, diagram sheets and the three-scientist reading/evidence sheet. Have Version 0 models ready.

DO
Introduce the lesson title briefly. The opening is included in the Predict allocation.

SAY
Cell theory — and what the cells in our diagrams share.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0 minutes

DO

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0 minutes

DO
Prepare before pupils arrive. Phase timings include the opening and closing work. Materials and notes support offline teaching.

IF…

TIME: 0.5 minutes

DO
Briefly link to the previous lesson and point to today. Keep later detailed mechanisms for the appropriate source lesson.

SAY
Last lesson we recorded our starting ideas about Amina’s cut.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0.75 minutes

DO
Introduce the three learning goals and process vocabulary. Do not explain the comparison before pupils predict.

SAY
We will use evidence to test our ideas and connect them to Amina’s healing finger.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

PREDICT PHASE (8 minutes total, including opening)
TIME: 4.5 minutes

DO
Give the full 3-minute silent writing period. Then pairs share for 90 seconds. Use a typical-cell comparison; platelets are fragments, not complete cells.

SAY
Think back to Amina’s finger. Write three sentences: I think all cells share… because…

WAIT TIME
3 full minutes of silent writing; 90 seconds of partner talk.

LOOK FOR
Every pupil has three starting sentences. Note membrane, DNA or control-centre ideas; flag blanks for support.

IF…
If a pupil writes I do not know, record that starting point and support them during diagram study; do not give the comparison now.

WHY THIS WORKS
Writing first preserves each pupil’s own starting point.

ANSWER KEY
This is an uncorrected starting prediction, not a test. Revisit after gathering evidence.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
Cold-call three pairs across the room. Record key words in a board column. Do not correct until evidence is available.

SAY
What did your pair agree on? Let us hold that idea and test it.

WAIT TIME
5–10 seconds before taking each answer.

LOOK FOR
Whose claims include a reason? Record recurring ideas without endorsing them.

IF…
If a pupil says every cell has a nucleus, write it as a prediction to test against the bacterial diagram.

WHY THIS WORKS
The visible list creates a record pupils can revise later.

ANSWER KEY
Record pupils’ own statements; no correct class list yet.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

OBSERVE PHASE (30 minutes total)
TIME: 8 minutes

DO
Groups of four draw a two-column mapping table. Use the five mappings in the key. Then discuss where the analogy fails. Check two tables per group.

SAY
A home kitchen in Kericho and a hospital canteen in Nairobi use familiar tools in different arrangements. Which feature controls entry?

WAIT TIME
10 seconds for reflection; 12 seconds after the membrane question.

LOOK FOR
At least five mappings; pupils distinguish recipe information from the place it is stored.

IF…
If pupils give a cell a thinking boss, state: Cell parts respond to chemical signals; a cell has no cook making decisions.

WHY THIS WORKS
A familiar analogy supports first ideas, but its limits prevent literal misconceptions.

ANSWER KEY
Door/boundary → cell membrane; recipe-book information → DNA (held in the nucleus in the eukaryotic example); jiko → mitochondria; sufuria, mwiko and chopping board → organelles. The utensils are not assigned separately to particular organelles. Limits: kitchens have cooks, doors are not selectively permeable membranes, kitchens do not divide.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
The analogy applies to the eukaryotic example. Bacteria have no mitochondria or nucleus. A jiko is a rough energy-release analogy, not an identical process.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
Use the labelled drawing as evidence, not a real observation through a microscope. Pupils identify names before organelle functions are taught in Lessons 4–5.

SAY
Look for boundaries, the location of DNA and structures shared with the other drawings.

WAIT TIME
Allow a quiet scan before inviting observations.

LOOK FOR
Pupils use the actual labels and distinguish a nucleus from bacterial DNA.

IF…
If ribosomes are mistaken for membrane-bound compartments, point to the small dots and return to this during Explain.

ANSWER KEY
Typical animal: membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ER and ribosomes. Typical photosynthetic plant example also shows a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and large central vacuole. The bacterium has a peptidoglycan wall, membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and circular chromosome in a nucleoid, with no nuclear membrane.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
Representative drawings, not to scale. Not every specialised cell has every illustrated structure. Some E. coli strains cause illness, while many are harmless. Do not infer that all bacteria are pathogens.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
Read the short information cards before filling the evidence table on the next slide. Provide printed copies for reference while pupils write. These cards supply offline reading.

SAY
What did each scientist contribute, and how could the idea help us think about Amina’s finger?

WAIT TIME
Quiet reading, then move to the table.

LOOK FOR
Pupils locate a contribution for each scientist rather than copying a name only.

IF…
If reading is difficult, read each card aloud and let pupils point to the matching scientist.

ANSWER KEY
Schleiden: plant tissues are built from cells. Schwann: animal tissues are built from cells. Virchow: new cells arise from existing cells.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
The dates and attributions follow the supplied example: Schleiden 1838, Schwann 1839, Virchow 1855. These are selected historical contributions, not a claim that three people alone established cell theory.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 6 minutes

DO
Pupils complete each scientist row using the reading. The phenomenon-connection sentence is essential. Circulate without filling cells for them.

SAY
For each scientist, write how the idea connects to Amina’s healing finger.

WAIT TIME
Wait 10 seconds after individual prompts.

LOOK FOR
Every row includes a contribution and a meaningful connection; read one table per group.

IF…
For a blank connection ask the source prompt: Virchow said all cells come from pre-existing cells — how does that explain where new skin cells came from?

WHY THIS WORKS
The last column connects historical knowledge to an explanation.

ANSWER KEY
Schleiden, Germany/1838: plants are cellular; the onion Amina sliced consists of plant cells. Schwann, Germany/1839: animals are cellular; Amina’s skin is made of animal cells. Virchow, Germany/1855: new cells come from existing cells; existing skin cells divide to produce new cells during healing. These are source-derived connections, not direct evidence of division in the drawing.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 8 minutes

DO
Give 12 pre-cut cards per group. Sort into Prokaryote / Eukaryote. Put shared cards across the dividing line or copy them into both columns. Give 8 minutes; note disputes for Explain.

SAY
Use the diagrams. A feature can belong in both categories. Record your final arrangement.

WAIT TIME
8 minutes of group sorting.

LOOK FOR
Which groups put ribosomes only in eukaryotes? Are membrane and cytoplasm shared?

IF…
Do not announce disputed answers yet. Ask: Which diagram gives you evidence for that choice?

ANSWER KEY
Prokaryote example: nucleoid, bacterial cell, 1–5 μm, circular main chromosome. Eukaryote examples: nucleus, mitochondria, membrane-bound organelles, 10–100 μm, plant/animal/fungal cell. Both: ribosomes, cell membrane, cytoplasm. The size ranges are typical examples, not absolute classification tests.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

EXPLAIN PHASE (18 minutes total)
TIME: 3 minutes

DO
Revisit the predictions and disputed sort cards. Pupils mark confirmed/revised ideas in a new colour. Correct the actual misconception observed, not an assumed class error.

SAY
Ribosomes appear in both diagrams. That does not make the two cell types identical.

WAIT TIME
5–10 seconds after questions.

LOOK FOR
Pupils distinguish ribosomes from membrane-bound organelles and revise their own prior claims.

IF…
If ribosomes remain eukaryote-only, point to the bacterial dots and ask the pupil to update the card placement.

ANSWER KEY
Both examples show membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes. The bacterium has no membrane-bound nucleus; the eukaryotic examples do. Only the plant and bacterial examples have a wall, made from different materials.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
Ribosomes make proteins; their presence alone does not establish pathogenicity. The draft removes that implication from the example.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 3 minutes

DO
Consolidate the three source tenets. Connect the third to new skin cells; do not explain specialised healing roles yet.

SAY
Which idea explains where new skin cells came from?

WAIT TIME
10 seconds before answering.

LOOK FOR
Pupils connect existing cells with new cells rather than saying cells appear from nothing.

IF…
If pupils propose spontaneous appearance, return to the third tenet and the observed repair story.

ANSWER KEY
All organisms consist of one or more cells. A cell is the basic unit of living structure and function. New cells arise from existing cells. The third, associated here with Virchow, explains that new skin cells derive from existing cells.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 4 minutes

DO
Pupils annotate their diagram sheets, not the reference slide. Keep the source colour system consistent. Explain the cell-wall exception and distinguish the two materials.

SAY
Green means shared across the two broad cell categories; it does not mean every cell in every category has that structure.

WAIT TIME
Give pupils time to check label by label with a partner.

LOOK FOR
Ribosomes green; membrane and cytoplasm green. Plant and bacterial walls green, with materials noted; no animal wall. Chloroplasts and central vacuole red.

IF…
If the wall is called plant-only, compare the E. coli and plant labels. If nucleus is green, revisit the nucleoid.

ANSWER KEY
GREEN: membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and walls on the plant/bacterial examples only. BLUE: nucleus, mitochondria and ER in the eukaryotic examples. RED: chloroplasts and the large central vacuole on the plant example. Plant walls are cellulose; the E. coli wall includes peptidoglycan.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
The source uses category-level sharing; this requires an explicit exception for walls. Generic diagrams must not be presented as universal descriptions of specialised cells.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 8 minutes

DO
Give 6 full minutes of silent writing, then ask two pupils to read their work. Collect six notebooks, two from each ability group, for review.

SAY
Write four sentences. Make a claim, name the observed change, then use cell theory to explain it.

WAIT TIME
6 minutes silent writing. After readings, allow a brief class thumbs response on the reasoning.

LOOK FOR
A clear claim; observation from the illustrated story as evidence; cell theory used in reasoning with because/therefore.

IF…
If a pupil writes only Virchow as the evidence, ask: What change did the story show? Then ask what scientific idea explains it.

WHY THIS WORKS
An observation and an explanatory theory play different roles.

ANSWER KEY
Claim: new skin cells came from existing skin cells. Evidence: the story shows new skin appearing as the cut closes. Reasoning: because new cells arise from existing cells, existing skin cells divided to make new ones. Therefore new cells helped close the surface. The drawing illustrates appearance; it does not directly show division or migration.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
No photograph or observed edge-to-centre spreading is claimed: L1 used illustrative finger drawings. This is a careful limitation of the supplied CER exemplar.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

DRIVING QUESTION BOARD PHASE (8 minutes total)
TIME: 8 minutes

DO
Reread the driving question. Give 3 minutes silent reflection. Each pupil stars an answered/partly answered question and posts ONE note: question OR growing understanding. Read three or four notes and photograph the board.

SAY
What has today’s evidence helped us understand? What still puzzles you?

WAIT TIME
3 minutes of individual reflection.

LOOK FOR
Every pupil posts at least one note. Check green notes for the mistaken claim that all cells are identical.

IF…
If a note says all cells are the same, ask the pupil to name a difference visible in today’s diagrams and revise the note.

ANSWER KEY
Valid understanding: new cells come from existing cells; typical bacterial and body cells differ in nucleus/organelles. Valid wonder: a genuine unresolved question. Do not claim the full specialisation question is answered.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
The source asks one new note of either colour, not one of each. An additional evidence vote is not in the source and is flagged in the build log.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

MODEL BUILDING PHASE (12 minutes total)
TIME: 12 minutes

DO
Pupils use the same notebook record, dated Version 1. Give 10 minutes independent sketch/key work and 2 minutes partner limitation sharing. Collect all models for review; return next lesson.

SAY
The required labels are membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, and cell wall if you choose a plant cell. Other structures are optional at this stage.

WAIT TIME
10 minutes independent work; wait 10 seconds after a correction prompt.

LOOK FOR
Three required animal labels or four plant labels; role statements; at least two genuine limitations. Functions beyond the core are provisional ideas, revisited in L4–5.

IF…
If an animal model has a wall, ask: What did the animal diagram show? If the key only states a location, ask for the structure’s possible role.

ANSWER KEY
Membrane: boundary controlling movement in/out; nucleus: holds DNA; cytoplasm: internal material where many reactions occur; plant wall: rigid outer support. Optional structures need not be fully understood yet. Limitations are individual honest gaps, not a fixed answer.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
The V2 source requires 3–4 core labels, unlike the example’s longer compulsory list. Detailed functions are taught later. Language support from V2: confirm proposed Kiswahili terms with the school’s language teacher before use. Pupils may discuss in Kiswahili or a home language first, then English; accept a labelled drawing or spoken explanation where appropriate.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 4 minutes

DO
Pupils complete the lesson row. Bring the explanation back to Amina’s cut, then close with the next lesson teaser.

SAY
What did we observe? What did we learn? What can we now explain?

LOOK FOR
Answers refer to this lesson’s evidence and distinguish observations from ideas.

IF…
If the phenomenon link is absent, ask which comparison or theory idea helps explain Amina’s healing finger.

ANSWER KEY
observed: In this lesson, learners observed labelled diagrams of generalised animal cells, plant cells, and prokaryotic cells. They sorted structural feature cards into Prokaryote and Eukaryote categories and studied the ugali-kitchen analogy mapped onto cell structure components.
learned: Learners learned the three tenets of cell theory (all living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells arise from pre-existing cells) and the contributions of Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow. They learned the key structural differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, including the presence or absence of a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
explained: Learners explained, using a Claim–Evidence–Reasoning paragraph, how Virchow's tenet ('all cells from pre-existing cells') accounts for the production of new skin cells during the healing of Amina's finger. They also explained their Version 1 cell model using a labelled diagram with a structural-function key and articulated the limitations of their current model.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 2. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TEACHER REFLECTION
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions in your planner: (1) During the card sort, which features were most consistently misclassified — and does your Lesson 3 plan address those specific misconceptions? (2) Review the 6 collected CER paragraphs: did learners connect Virchow's tenet directly to new skin cell production, or did they write generically about cells? If the latter, plan a 5-minute CER revisit at the start of Lesson 3. (3) Count the ratio of yellow (question) to green (understanding) DQB notes: if yellow heavily outnumbers green, learners may need a consolidation activity before Lesson 3 advances to cell specialisation. (4) Scan the Version 1 models: are animal cells being drawn with cell walls? Is the nucleus consistently represented as membrane-bound? Patterns across the class should inform your Lesson 3 opening correction sequence. (5) Reflect on wait time: did you hold the full 10–12 seconds, or did you answer for learners? Longer wait time consistently produces more complete learner responses — practise holding silence even when it feels uncomfortable.
